> ## Kept deliberately as a record of superseded reasoning
>
> **The active pitch is `results/pitch_v2_tpa_readout.md`. All revisions go
> there. Do not edit this file.**
>
> This document is retained on purpose, not by neglect. It is the second of two
> framings that collapsed on contact with the literature, and it is more useful
> as a record of *how* they collapsed than it would be deleted.
>
> **What was wrong with it, in order of severity:**
>
> 1. **Its central ask was already answered.** It asks whether TphC's clamshell
>    closure can transduce a signal. TPAsense (bioRxiv 2026) had already built
>    exactly that — TphC-iV283–sf-cpGFP, Kd 99 nM, ΔF/F −0.45 — plus a patent.
>    I asserted "nobody appears to have tested this" **without searching**.
> 2. **The CAR architecture could not have worked.** TphC cannot bind PET
>    (aromatic esters do not bind; PET is a polyester), and a soluble monovalent
>    ligand cannot cluster a CAR to trigger signalling.
> 3. **It targeted the wrong bottleneck.** Macrophages already phagocytose
>    microplastics efficiently (Tim4). Accumulated particles are what suppress
>    efferocytosis — so a receptor that increases uptake would worsen the lesion.
> 4. **It still cites selectivity numbers that are docking artefacts** (+0.96
>    kcal/mol vs hippurate). Six of six panel decoys are experimentally
>    non-binding compounds.
>
> **The pattern worth remembering:** every failure above came from building
> first and checking prior art afterwards. Both this pitch and the one before it
> were internally careful — replicates, controls, error bars, explicit caveats —
> and both were aimed at questions that were already settled. Rigour applied to
> the wrong question does not rescue it.
>
> See `week3_docking_vs_experiment.md`, `week3_architecture_analysis.md`, and
> `week3_prior_art_check.md` for the evidence.

---

## The goal

A CAR-macrophage that recognises terephthalate — the primary breakdown product
of PET — as a route to clearing microplastic burden from human tissue.
**TphC** (*Comamonas* sp., PDB 7NDS) is the natural terephthalate receptor and
the obvious candidate recognition domain.

Two things must be true for that to work. One is established. The other is not
addressed anywhere in the literature I can find, and it is where I would like
help.

---

## What is already established (not my work)

Gautom et al. 2021 (*Nat Commun* 12:6244):

| | |
|---|---|
| Terephthalate Kd (ITC) | **0.364 µM** |
| Specificity | narrow — six-membered **para-substituted aromatic dicarboxylate** required |
| Monocarboxylates (44 compounds incl. benzoate-like) | do not bind |
| ortho/meta regioisomers | do not bind |
| Mechanism | clamshell closure, ~36° domain rotation on ligand binding |

**Recognition is solved.** The affinity is good and the specificity is sharp.

---

## The two open questions

### Q1 (primary) — does ligand binding *transduce*?

TphC is a periplasmic solute-binding protein. Its natural job is to bind
terephthalate and hand it to a membrane transporter — **not** to generate a
signal. A CAR ectodomain must convert a binding event into receptor clustering
or a conformational change that reaches the intracellular signalling domain.

TphC undergoes a large, well-characterised **~36° clamshell closure** on
binding. That is a promising mechanical starting point, but nobody appears to
have tested whether it can drive CAR-style signalling.

**This is the actual engineering risk, and it is untested.**

### Q2 (secondary) — is 0.364 µM sufficient *in vivo*?

Required receptor occupancy depends on tissue terephthalate concentration.
Urinary TPA is well measured (median 70 ng/mL ≈ 0.42 µM, 100% detection,
n = 30). **Plasma and tissue concentrations are not published.** If tissue TPA
is ≈ 0.4 µM, a 0.364 µM binder sits near half-occupancy — workable. If it is
100× lower, affinity maturation becomes necessary before anything else matters.

---

## The ask

I would value **either** of these, and both are bounded:

**Option A — a transduction test (higher value).** Express TphC as a CAR
ectodomain in a reporter line (Jurkat-NFAT or a macrophage model) and test
whether soluble terephthalate, or terephthalate presented on a PET particle
surface, drives signalling. This is the question that decides whether the whole
approach is viable.

**Option B — a concentration measurement (cheaper).** Quantify terephthalate in
human plasma or tissue by LC-MS/MS. Methods for urine are published and would
transfer. This is a small analytical study that would also stand alone as a
biomonitoring contribution.

I am not asking for co-authorship, funding, or a long-term commitment — I am
asking whether either experiment is worth a student rotation or a spare slot,
and I am glad to send all data and code first so you can judge for yourself.

## Finding 1 — a docking failure case worth knowing about

I built a selectivity benchmark before checking the experimental literature.
Against the 61-compound DSF/ITC ground truth, my pipeline:

| | |
|---|---|
| Error on the true ligand | **+0.73 kcal/mol** (good) |
| Non-binders classified as credible binders | **6 of 6**, implied Kd 3–38 µM |
| True selectivity margin understated by | **2.8–4.1 kcal/mol** (reported ~3×; truth >275×) |

The error is **asymmetric**: accurate on the real binder, badly over-predicting
non-binders. The reason is structural — an empirical scoring function has no
term for *"this ligand lacks a required pharmacophore."* A benzene ring plus one
carboxylate collects most of terephthalate's contact score; what the function
cannot express is that the second *para* carboxylate is obligatory, because
TphC is a **two-point recognition device** and a one-point ligand fails
regardless of how well its single point fits.

I suspect this generalises to other two-point-recognition sites, and that the
signature — a compressed score distribution where everything ligand-shaped lands
within 1–2 kcal/mol of the target — is diagnostic of it.

**The lesson I took:** I validated *pose prediction* (redocking gate) and then
relied on *cross-ligand affinity ranking*. Those are different tasks with
different error profiles, and I never validated the second. The data to do so
existed in the paper I got my structure from.

---

## Honest limitations

- I am [self-taught / a high school student / etc.] working independently.
- My selectivity conclusions were wrong and I have retracted them above; the
  corrected analysis is what I am presenting.
- No experimental validation of anything I have done.
- Conformational dynamics are untested: hinge-adjacent residues were excluded
  from all modelling because ESMFold could not reproduce the closed-pocket
  geometry (4.014 Å RMSD, concentrated at the domain interface). Since Q1 is
  fundamentally a dynamics question, this is a real gap in what I can offer.
